jokes.explanation: The walk-off concept is pure absurdist gold — the idea that a fashion walk is a formal competitive discipline with codified rules, adjudicated by David Bowie, perfectly satirizes fashion world pretension. The gravity of delivery elevates it beyond a simple sight gag.

jokes.text: Age before beauty, goat cheese. / Whatever.
jokes.setup: Derek and Hansel must decide who walks first; Derek delivers a pointed insult ('goat cheese' implying Hansel smells or is a hick)
jokes.punchline: Hansel's utterly unbothered 'Whatever' — he is so cool and unflappable that even a direct insult lands as meaningless
jokes.explanation: Perfect character economy. 'Goat cheese' as an insult is weird enough to be funny on its own; Hansel's one-word dismissal is exactly on-brand for his California-zen persona. The contrast between Derek's pettiness and Hansel's cool is the entire joke, and it's delivered in four words total.

jokes.text: Playschool, baby.
jokes.setup: Derek has just completed his opening walk, presumably with his best moves
jokes.punchline: Hansel dismisses it as child's play — 'Playschool, baby' — a casually devastating taunt delivered mid-performance
jokes.explanation: Two words that do maximum work. Hansel's whole character is effortless superiority, and 'Playschool, baby' epitomizes it. The 'baby' tacked on adds just the right condescension. Works best visually alongside Hansel's walk, which we can infer is spectacular.

jokes.text: You got to cut me. I can't see. I'm blind out there. Evian. Evian.
jokes.setup: Derek is performing in a walk-off, struggling to keep up with Hansel
jokes.punchline: Derek between rounds, treating a fashion walk like a boxing match — demanding to be 'cut' and calling for Evian water like it's smelling salts
jokes.explanation: The boxing corner metaphor applied to a fashion walk is a rich vein the film mines brilliantly here. 'I'm blind out there' as though the runway is a ring, plus the specific brand-name 'Evian' (not just water — the most pretentious water), is sharp character comedy. The escalating panic before 'Evian. Evian.' lands the laugh.

jokes.text: Where am I? Where am I? / Kickin', Hoss. / I'm going monk.
jokes.setup: Derek is disoriented after his walk, still in boxing-corner mode
jokes.punchline: His trainer assures him he's 'Kickin', Hoss' and Derek's response is to announce he's 'going monk' — an utterly absurd spiritual declaration mid-competition
jokes.explanation: Continues the boxing parody setup effectively. 'Going monk' is an odd enough phrase to generate a laugh, though it's a setup for the more elaborate prayer bit that follows.

jokes.text: I got to go monk. Prayer. Prayer. Pray to the Great Spirit.
jokes.setup: Derek declares he's 'going monk' between rounds of the walk-off
jokes.punchline: His spiritual preparation involves a vague, pan-religious mash-up that reveals he has no actual spiritual tradition — 'Pray to the Great Spirit' is cartoonishly generic
jokes.explanation: Derek's vapid spirituality is a character note that lands. The specificity of 'Great Spirit' (a Native American concept, delivered by a New Jersey himbo) captures his cultural illiteracy perfectly.

jokes.text: Why is he sticking his hand in his pants?
jokes.setup: Hansel is performing some mysterious move in the walk-off
jokes.punchline: The innocent confusion of an onlooker asking the obvious question about whatever bizarre physical maneuver Hansel is doing, treating the audience as proxy for the viewer
jokes.explanation: The setup-and-innocent-question structure is well-executed. We (and the crowd) have no idea what Hansel is doing, and the guileless query captures the absurdity perfectly. It also serves as a setup for the ultimate reveal.

jokes.text: That's what I'm talking about. / Derek, you're not a kid any more. You could hurt yourself out there.
jokes.setup: Hansel has apparently done something extraordinary in the walk-off
jokes.punchline: Mike Tyson, appearing as Derek's concerned corner man, warning him about the physical dangers of the fashion walk as though it were a boxing match
jokes.explanation: The casting of Mike Tyson as a fashion walk corner man is inherently funny — the most famously violent boxer in the world giving earnest concern about the physical toll of modelling. The line 'you could hurt yourself out there' applied to a runway walk is perfect tonal absurdism.

jokes.text: Thank God I wore underwear today.
jokes.setup: Derek is steeling himself to go back out into the walk-off
jokes.punchline: His pre-performance affirmation is relief that he's wearing underwear — implying he often doesn't, and that this oversight nearly cost him
jokes.explanation: One of the funniest lines in this section. It works on multiple levels: it's a perfect character note (Derek routinely goes commando), it's incongruously casual given the competitive stakes, and 'thank God' implies a sincere moment of gratitude about his underwear choices. Maximum economy — nine words, big laugh.

jokes.text: Disqualified.
jokes.setup: Derek has apparently pulled off some spectacular move — the crowd is cheering, the tension is high
jokes.punchline: Bowie's single, flat, unemotional 'Disqualified' — delivered after what seemed like a triumphant moment, with no explanation
jokes.explanation: One word doing maximal comedic work. The pacing — the visual climax of Derek's desperate move, the crowd reaction, then Bowie's flat, bored 'Disqualified' — is a masterclass in comedic deflation. Perfect economy score of 10: not one syllable wasted. The deadpan authority of Bowie as judge makes it land harder.

jokes.text: I think Katinka wants to kill you. / Good. I deserve to die if I can't beat Han-suck-ass in a walk-off.
jokes.setup: Derek has just lost the walk-off and is being consoled; Matilda drops an almost offhand warning about Katinka
jokes.punchline: Derek's sulky non-reaction to being told someone wants to kill him — his wounded pride over losing to 'Han-suck-ass' overrides his survival instinct entirely
jokes.explanation: The reveal that someone wants to kill Derek is played entirely for the contrast with his petty vanity. 'Han-suck-ass' is a great Derek portmanteau insult — childish, specific, and perfectly in-character for someone who cannot process a threat to his life as more important than his modelling reputation.

jokes.text: The guy had to miraculously pull his underwear out of his butt just to beat you.
jokes.setup: Derek is despondent about losing the walk-off
jokes.punchline: Matilda's consolation reveals the shocking detail of Hansel's winning move — the hand-in-pants mystery is finally explained: he was executing a miraculous underwear extraction
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff to the 'hand in pants' setup and it's genuinely exceptional. The word 'miraculously' is key — it frames a wedgie removal as a divine athletic feat. The structure is perfect: planted mystery, delayed reveal, and the consolation framing means we learn what happened at the most emotionally resonant moment. Among the best gags in the reel.

jokes.text: And all he had to do was turn left.
jokes.setup: Matilda is building on her consolation — Hansel had to perform a miracle just to win
jokes.punchline: The addition of 'and all he had to do was turn left' — implying a simple directional turn was Derek's undoing, setting up the revelation of his condition
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical setup line that seems like a minor observation but is actually a perfect plant for one of the film's best running gags. 'All he had to do' makes it sound easy, maximizing Derek's humiliation before the revelation.

jokes.text: I'm not an ambi-turner. It's a problem I had since I was a baby. I can't turn left.
jokes.setup: Matilda mentions turning left; Derek goes quiet and confessional
jokes.punchline: Derek reveals with complete sincerity that he is physically incapable of turning left — a 'condition' he's had since birth, delivered with the gravity of a medical disclosure
jokes.explanation: One of the film's signature jokes and it earns that status. 'Ambi-turner' is a neologism that perfectly apes medical terminology, delivering the absurd concept with academic legitimacy. The escalation — 'since I was a baby' — adds pathos. It's also structurally flawless: the left turn has just been planted as the pivotal issue, and Derek's confession recontextualizes the entire walk-off. This is a 9+ level joke in the film's canon.

jokes.text: Derek, that's nothing to be ashamed of. I'm sure there are a lot of people out there who can't turn... [long pause] I mean, there have got to be some people out there, just like you, who can't turn... [longer pause] Turn left.
jokes.setup: Matilda begins to offer reassurance that Derek's condition is common
jokes.punchline: She clearly cannot think of a single other person who can't turn left; her pauses grow longer and more uncomfortable as she searches for a comparison that doesn't exist
jokes.explanation: A masterfully timed awkward silence gag. The structure — confident opening, increasing pause, flustered ending — is structurally impeccable. The comedy comes entirely from the timing: Matilda's earnest attempt to normalize Derek's condition runs directly into the wall of its absolute uniqueness. The two extended pauses (marked in the transcript) are the punchlines.

jokes.text: "Derriere Extraordinaire."
jokes.setup: Derek and the mysterious figure are walking through a cemetery of male models who died young; each gravestone has an epitaph
jokes.punchline: A male model's epitaph reading 'Derriere Extraordinaire' — his greatest achievement and legacy was his remarkable butt
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy working well. A gravestone epitaph in a cemetery dedicated to male models who died young, and the best thing anyone could say about this man was his butt. The French phrasing adds pomposity that makes the deflation funnier. Economical visual gag.

jokes.text: 92 minus 63.
jokes.setup: Walking through the cemetery, checking lifespans of dead male models
jokes.punchline: Derek doing math out loud to calculate a model's age — the implication being he literally cannot process numbers without subtracting them, and also that 29 years old is the grim ceiling for these men
jokes.explanation: A quiet character-comedy beat — Derek's dim arithmetic done aloud. It's functional rather than spectacular, but it characterizes him efficiently.

jokes.text: None of them ever made it past 30. I did. / Are you a ghost?
jokes.setup: J.P. reveals the grim pattern of male models dying before 30, then notes he survived
jokes.punchline: Derek's immediate follow-up question — 'Are you a ghost?' — is the dimmest possible interpretation of a dramatic revelation
jokes.explanation: A precision Derek-stupidity joke. J.P. sets up with gravitas — 'none of them made it past 30, I did' — and Derek's mind goes immediately to the supernatural rather than logical explanation. It's character-perfect and structurally tight. 'Are you a ghost?' is instantly quotable and captures Derek's whole deal in three words.

jokes.text: And behind every hit, a card-carrying male model.
jokes.setup: J.P. is laying out his grand conspiracy theory about the fashion industry behind political assassinations
jokes.punchline: The bureaucratic specificity of 'card-carrying male model' — as though the assassin's union issues membership cards — applied to murder
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'card-carrying' applied to a fashion-industry assassination ring is a good joke — it borrows the McCarthy-era phrasing and applies it to a secret society of male model killers. Solid absurdist world-building.

jokes.text: Okay, that's impossible. / Oh, yeah? Listen and learn, sweetness.
jokes.setup: J.P. claims fashion designers have been behind every major political assassination for 200 years
jokes.punchline: J.P.'s 'Listen and learn, sweetness' — a conspiratorial mentor who calls his pupil 'sweetness' while delivering world-historical bombshells
jokes.explanation: The term of endearment 'sweetness' deployed in this context is a mild character note for J.P. — slightly flamboyant, slightly condescending. Functional but not especially original.

jokes.text: Abe Lincoln wanted to abolish slavery, right? But who do you think made the powdered wigs and coloured leg stockings, worn by our country's early leaders? Mugatu! Slaves, Derek.
jokes.setup: J.P. is about to explain the Lincoln assassination through the fashion conspiracy lens
jokes.punchline: The conspiracy logic runs: Lincoln threatened slavery → slaves made fashion accessories → Mugatu needed slaves → Mugatu had Lincoln killed. The punchline 'Slaves, Derek' is delivered as a triumphant reveal of this insane chain of reasoning
jokes.explanation: One of the film's sharpest absurdist-conspiracy bits. The logic is internally consistent and completely insane simultaneously. 'Mugatu!' shouted as though it's the obvious missing piece, followed by the flat 'Slaves, Derek' — said as a summary to a dimwit — is very well constructed. The jump from Lincoln's assassination to fashion accessories is a genuinely original comedic idea.

jokes.text: So the powers that be hired John Wilkes Booth, the original model/actor, to do Mr Lincoln in.
jokes.setup: J.P. continues the fashion-conspiracy historical narrative
jokes.punchline: John Wilkes Booth reframed as 'the original model/actor' — a hyphenate celebrity career that culminated in presidential assassination
jokes.explanation: The 'model/actor' hyphenate is a brilliant satirical touch — it perfectly mocks the Hollywood career path while recontextualizing a historical monster as a showbiz type. 'The original model/actor' implies a lineage of ambitious types who leverage their looks into other careers. Very sharp.

jokes.text: Kennedy had just put a trade embargo on Cuba, ostensibly halting the shipment of Cuban-manufactured slacks. Incredibly popular item at the time.
jokes.setup: J.P. pivots to the JFK assassination, describing geopolitical events in fashion terms
jokes.punchline: The Cuban Missile Crisis / trade embargo reframed as a slacks-supply crisis, with the editorializing 'Incredibly popular item at the time' as though speaking about a seasonal collection
jokes.explanation: The recontextualization of the Cuban trade embargo as a slacks crisis is excellent historical absurdism. 'Ostensibly' is a perfect word choice — implying official cover stories — before the reveal that the actual crisis was trouser supply. 'Incredibly popular item at the time' as an aside, like a footnote in a fashion catalogue, is comic gold.

jokes.text: Lee Harvey Oswald was not a male model. / You're God damn right he wasn't. But those two lookers who capped Kennedy from the grassy knoll sure as shit were.
jokes.setup: Derek raises the obvious objection: Oswald wasn't a model
jokes.punchline: J.P. not only agrees but pivots to the grassy knoll theory — the real killers were 'two lookers,' i.e., handsome male models, as though physical attractiveness is the key piece of assassination evidence
jokes.explanation: One of the best gags in the section. Derek's logical objection is precisely the right question, and J.P.'s answer doubles down brilliantly — not only confirming the grassy knoll theory but adding the qualifier that the shooters were 'lookers.' The word 'lookers' (fashion slang for attractive people) applied to assassins is a perfect tonal collision. 'Sure as shit were' has great conviction.

jokes.text: I can't get over... / Wait a minute. / No. / I know that hand.
jokes.setup: A phone rings and is answered by someone passing by (apparently a stranger); J.P. and Derek observe the hand
jokes.punchline: Derek or J.P. (likely J.P.) recognizing a stranger purely by their hand — establishing that J.P. is so obsessed with hands that he has encyclopedic knowledge of them
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the hand-model reveal. The beat of recognizing someone from their hand alone — when the rest of us would recognize a face — is a good character-specific absurdism that pays off nicely.

jokes.text: It was in the fall 1973 Bulova watch catalogue.
jokes.setup: J.P. has identified someone by their hand; now he explains how
jokes.punchline: The specific, archival precision of 'fall 1973 Bulova watch catalogue' — J.P. has memorized decades of watch catalogues in order to identify hands on sight
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character-integration score because this detail could ONLY belong to a hand model — it's not just funny, it's world-building comedy. The specificity ('fall 1973,' 'Bulova') makes it funnier than a generic answer would be. It suggests J.P. has a Rain Man-level catalogue of hands committed to memory. Among the stronger jokes in this reel.

jokes.text: Thanks to this homemade hyperbaric chamber, my sweet baby never did.
jokes.setup: J.P. reveals he is the world's greatest hand model; someone notes that things change
jokes.punchline: J.P. gestures to a homemade hyperbaric chamber he uses to preserve his hands, calling them 'my sweet baby' — the singular dedication of a man who treats his hands as a beloved infant
jokes.explanation: The homemade hyperbaric chamber for hand preservation is the kind of absurdist visual detail that the film deploys brilliantly. 'My sweet baby' referring to his hands (singular, as a collective noun baby) while gesturing to what must be a ridiculous DIY pressure vessel is superb character work. The commitment to the bit is what elevates it.

jokes.text: So, how did you manage to escape? / Because I'm a hand model, mama. A finger jockey. We don't think the same way as the face and body boys do. We're a different breed.
jokes.setup: J.P. reveals he was scheduled to assassinate Jimmy Carter; someone asks how he escaped the brainwashing
jokes.punchline: His escape is attributed to being a 'finger jockey' — hand models, apparently, have a fundamentally different cognitive makeup from face-and-body models, which made them immune to the programming
jokes.explanation: 'Finger jockey' is an inspired coinage — the racetrack/rodeo metaphor applied to hand modelling creates a whole subculture of physical specialists with their own slang and pride. 'We don't think the same way as the face and body boys' creates a taxonomy of model types with implied class distinctions. 'We're a different breed' as a sincere statement of hand-model superiority is perfect.

jokes.text: Male models are genetically constructed to become assassins. They're in peak physical condition. They can gain entry to the most secure places in the world. And most important of all, models don't think for themselves. They do as they're told. / That is not true. / Yes, it is, Derek. / Okay.
jokes.setup: J.P. is making the case for why male models make ideal assassins, culminating in 'models don't think for themselves'
jokes.punchline: Derek's reflexive 'That is not true' — immediately followed by his instant capitulation 'Okay' the moment J.P. confirms it — is the ultimate self-own proving J.P.'s point
jokes.explanation: One of the best structured jokes in the film. The setup ('models don't think for themselves, they do as they're told') is the thesis; Derek's protest is the expected counter-reaction; but his immediate 'Okay' the moment J.P. says 'Yes it is' is the perfect proof of concept. He literally does as he's told, confirming the accusation in real time. Structurally impeccable, completely character-integrated, and achieves maximum comedy with four words ('That is not true / Okay'). Comparable to anchor examples for craft.

jokes.text: You're a monkey, Derek! You're a monkey. Dance, monkey, in your little spangly shoes! Mash your cymbals, chimpy! Dance, Derek, dance! / Good point.
jokes.setup: J.P. is making the point that Derek just follows orders like a performing animal; to illustrate, he breaks into a full tirade
jokes.punchline: The escalation of the monkey metaphor into 'spangly shoes' and 'Mash your cymbals, chimpy!' getting increasingly unhinged — and Derek's response is simply 'Good point,' treating this unhinged abuse as a valid intellectual argument
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'monkey' to 'spangly shoes' to 'Mash your cymbals, chimpy!' is a great comedy of escalation — J.P. gets more unhinged with each beat. The best part is Derek's 'Good point' ending: not angry, not hurt, genuinely persuaded. He has taken 'you are a performing organ-grinder monkey' as a compliment or at least a valid observation.

jokes.text: But why male models? / Are you serious? I just... I just told you that a moment ago. / Right.
jokes.setup: J.P. has just delivered an extensive, persuasive explanation of why male models make ideal assassins
jokes.punchline: Derek immediately asks 'But why male models?' — the exact question that was just answered — and J.P.'s horrified 'Are you serious? I just told you that a moment ago' is perfect
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel and one of the best in the film. The setup is a lengthy, earnest explanation; the punchline is Derek asking the identical question that was just answered. J.P.'s exasperated response — delivered with barely contained disbelief — is perfect. The 'Right' Derek adds confirms he still doesn't get it. This is Airplane!-level comedy of repetition and dimwittedness: the joke works on first viewing and on every rewatch because knowing it's coming makes the inevitability funny. The economy is phenomenal — the entire joke is 15 words and relies on everything that came before it.

jokes.text: At the proper moment, they'll trigger you, usually using some kind of auditory or visual Pavlovian response mechanism. / 'Audi-what-ey'?
jokes.setup: J.P. explains the technical mechanism of brainwashing
jokes.punchline: Derek's 'Audi-what-ey?' — a phonetic approximation of a word he's never heard, delivered with genuine bafflement
jokes.explanation: 'Audi-what-ey?' is a great character-stupidity phonetic gag — Derek's brain can't parse 'auditory' so it goes to its most literal phonetic interpretation. The '-ey' suffix makes it funnier, implying he's guessing the ending. Pure Derek.

jokes.text: And when it's over— / What? / There's an after party?
jokes.setup: J.P. is about to explain what happens after Derek is triggered to assassinate someone
jokes.punchline: Derek interprets 'it's over' as meaning an event has concluded, and immediately asks about the after party — his brain defaults to social event logistics when confronted with assassination planning
jokes.explanation: 'There's an after party?' is a beautifully timed misdirection gag. J.P. is building to a dark revelation (presumably Derek will be killed after the hit), and Derek's mind goes to social logistics. The question mark is crucial — it's hopeful, almost enthusiastic. Perfect character integration: of course this is where Derek's mind goes. High quotability, great economy.

jokes.text: Good luck to you, Derek. I've always been a fan of Blue Steel. And I hear Magnum is gonna blow us all away.
jokes.setup: J.P. is parting from Derek as assassins close in; it's a dramatic farewell moment
jokes.punchline: In what may be his final words, J.P. chooses to comment on Derek's modelling looks — 'Blue Steel' and 'Magnum' — with the earnest investment of a true fan; 'blow us all away' is both fashion hyperbole and ominous given the context
jokes.explanation: A good farewell gag — J.P. prioritizes fashion commentary over survival, and 'blow us all away' works double as fashion enthusiasm and literal threat. The reference to Magnum as a payoff to the ongoing Magnum thread is well-placed.

jokes.text: Good luck to you, Derek. I've always been a fan of Blue Steel. And I hear Magnum is gonna blow us all away.
jokes.setup: J.P. is shot and dying; he uses his last breath to offer parting words to Derek
jokes.punchline: His dying words are not wisdom or a final clue — they are fashion-industry gossip about Derek's signature looks, specifically hype about the unreleased 'Magnum' look
jokes.explanation: A dying man's final words being fashion critique and anticipatory hype for a runway look is a perfect tonal joke. It also plants the Magnum payoff for later. 'Blow us all away' applied to a fashion look is good ironic word choice given the assassination context.

jokes.text: That she-male Katinka's not messing around. / You're telling me! For a second there, I thought someone was gonna be reading our 'eugoogoly.'
jokes.setup: Derek and Matilda have just escaped an assassination attempt
jokes.punchline: 'Eugoogoly' — Derek's mispronunciation of 'eulogy,' a callback to his established speech-giving incompetence from earlier in the film
jokes.explanation: 'Eugoogoly' as a malapropism/running gag earns well because it's character-specific and the context (he nearly died) makes the callback land with both comedic and dramatic weight. The mispronunciation is so wrong it suggests Derek has never encountered the word in written form.

jokes.text: For a second there, I thought someone was gonna be reading our 'eugoogoly.'
jokes.setup: Derek and Matilda have escaped the attack and are reflecting on how close they came to dying
jokes.punchline: Derek mispronounces 'eulogy' as 'eugoogoly' — an absurd malapropism that completely transforms the word, delivered with the confidence of someone who believes this is the correct pronunciation
jokes.explanation: A running gag callback that works beautifully. 'Eugoogoly' is one of the film's most quotable coinages — the specific rendering of 'eulogy' into something that sounds vaguely Greek and completely wrong is inspired. The callback to earlier eulogy jokes makes it resonate more deeply. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: I hate Hansel! Hansel, Hansel! Everywhere I look! Hansel! Hansel, Hansel!
jokes.setup: Derek has been asked to think of the last place anyone would look for him
jokes.punchline: Derek's mental process for finding a safe house consists entirely of a Hansel-fixated meltdown — the question requires strategic thought but instead produces unhinged jealousy
jokes.explanation: A good character beat — Derek's jealousy of Hansel is so all-consuming that it hijacks a life-or-death problem-solving moment. The escalation of 'Hansel!' repeated with increasing mania is well-performed but the joke itself is relatively simple.

jokes.text: Derek has been brainwashed to kill the prime minister of Malaysia. / And?
jokes.setup: Matilda delivers what should be a shocking revelation to Hansel about Derek's situation
jokes.punchline: Hansel's 'And?' — total nonchalance about a friend being brainwashed to commit political assassination, as though Matilda is building to the actual concerning part
jokes.explanation: One word doing maximum work. 'And?' captures Hansel's entire character — so laid-back and accepting that political assassination of a world leader is not a conversation-stopper. Perfect economy (1 word), strong character integration, and the structural timing is impeccable. A very good joke.

jokes.text: Derek said this would probably be the last place anyone would look for him. / Yeah, you're cool to hide here.
jokes.setup: Matilda explains why they came to Hansel's place — Derek's enemy's home is the last place anyone would look
jokes.punchline: Hansel's instant, unquestioning 'Yeah, you're cool to hide here' — his magnanimity with someone who just lost a bitter competition against him is part of his whole effortlessly cool character
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat — Hansel's complete lack of grudge-holding is funny given Derek's intense resentment. But it's setup for the reconciliation scene rather than a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: Fine. / Why you been acting so messed up towards me? [extended silence]
jokes.setup: Hansel agrees to shelter Derek but insists they 'straighten some shit out'; he asks why Derek has been acting messed up
jokes.punchline: The long, uncomfortable silence as Derek apparently has no answer, followed by 'Well, you go first' — a classic avoidance move in what was supposed to be Derek's confrontation
jokes.explanation: The awkward silence beat works because Derek clearly cannot process the emotional question asked of him, and his 'Well, you go first' deflection is very in-character. A gentle character-comedy beat.

jokes.text: And I felt like when you told me to Dere-lick my balls, that really hurt.
jokes.setup: Hansel is in the middle of a sincere emotional confession about how Derek's earlier insults hurt him
jokes.punchline: The completely sincere delivery of 'Dere-lick my balls' as a legitimately hurtful thing to say — the portmanteau insult from earlier in the film being replayed with genuine emotional weight
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Dere-lick my balls' is well-deployed here because it's played sincerely — Hansel treats this ridiculous invented insult as a genuine wound. The juxtaposition of a sentimental confession scene and the absurdity of that specific insult is good tonal comedy.

jokes.text: Your work in the winter '95 International Male catalogue made me want to be a model.
jokes.setup: Hansel is about to make a confession to Derek in the middle of their reconciliation
jokes.punchline: The 'International Male catalogue' — a notoriously campy mail-order menswear catalogue — as the artistic inspiration that launched Hansel's career; and the extended pause before the reveal heightens the absurdity
jokes.explanation: 'International Male catalogue' is a very specific, very funny cultural reference — it was an infamous catalogue known for its outrageous, campy menswear. Placing it as the artistic catalyst for the world's greatest male model is a great joke. The 'winter '95' specificity (echoing J.P.'s 'fall 1973') adds extra absurdist precision.

jokes.text: Your work in the winter '95 International Male catalogue made me want to be a model.
jokes.setup: In a sincere moment, Hansel reveals what inspired him to become a model
jokes.punchline: His inspirational turning point is 'the winter '95 International Male catalogue' — International Male being a mail-order catalog known for aggressively homoerotic and cheesy menswear, an utterly undignified inspiration source delivered with the reverence of citing a great master's work
jokes.explanation: Excellent specific-reference joke. The 'International Male catalogue' is a perfect choice — it was real, campy, and absolutely the cheesiest possible fashion inspiration. Calling it 'winter '95' as a specific issue (echoing Derek's 'fall 1973 Bulova' detail) adds to the absurdist precision. The gap between the reverent tone and the trashy inspiration is the whole joke.

jokes.text: I'll round up the troops here. Hey, what's up, y'all? This is Derek and Matilda. Derek, you know Natani and Chloe. Hi! We got Buzzy Sullivan, big wave surfer from Maverick's. Hey, bra. This is this fantastic band, the Little Kings, I met when I was ice sailing in Finland. That's my Sherpa, Lapsang.
jokes.setup: Hansel says he'll 'round up the troops' in his apartment to help Derek
jokes.punchline: His 'troops' turn out to be a rotating cast of eclectic globally-sourced companions: a big wave surfer, a Finnish band, and a Sherpa — the ensemble reveals Hansel's lifestyle as a kind of bohemian fantasy of extreme multiculturalism
jokes.explanation: The roster of Hansel's 'troops' is a good character-world-building joke — the specific detail of a Sherpa named Lapsang living in what appears to be a Soho loft, plus a band 'met ice sailing in Finland,' is a good accumulation of Hansel's impossibly cool globe-trotting life. The 'Hey, bra' from the surfer is a small additional beat.

jokes.text: Derek and Matilda are in hiding 'cause some dudes brainwashed Derek to off the prime minister of Micronesia. / Malaysia. / Right.
jokes.setup: Hansel is briefing his assembled companions on Derek's situation
jokes.punchline: He gets the country wrong — 'Micronesia' instead of 'Malaysia' — and accepts the correction with zero self-consciousness
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean character-comedy beat. Hansel's casual 'Right' after the correction is perfect — not embarrassed, not trying to cover. The specific wrong answer 'Micronesia' is funnier than a more obvious error because it shows he was at least in the right region.

jokes.text: This... This is really strong tea. / No, it's just right. Trust me.
jokes.setup: Hansel has served a special tea (fetched by his various companions) to help Derek and Matilda relax
jokes.punchline: Matilda immediately notices the tea is alarming in its potency; Hansel dismisses her concern — the tea is clearly hallucinogenic or at least extremely intoxicating
jokes.explanation: Setup for the later group nudity payoff. 'No, it's just right. Trust me' is a classic drug-dealer/yoga-teacher response from Hansel, well-characterized. Stronger in retrospect than on first viewing.

jokes.text: You know, Matilda, I'm surprised you're so worried about 'Der-rock.'
jokes.setup: Hansel is about to reference a magazine article about Matilda's feelings toward male models
jokes.punchline: His mispronunciation of 'Derek' as 'Der-rock' — a small but perfectly chosen character note suggesting Hansel has casually mispronounced the name of his arch-rival for years without being corrected
jokes.explanation: 'Der-rock' is a small, funny character detail — Hansel mishearing a name he's heard a thousand times. Probably funnier in performance than on the page, but it's a good, quick character note.

jokes.text: I think they're vain, stupid and incredibly self-centred. / I totally agree with you. But how do you feel about male models?
jokes.setup: Hansel asks why Matilda hates models; she answers sincerely about their vanity and stupidity
jokes.punchline: Hansel's 'I totally agree with you' — spoken as a male model — immediately followed by 'But how do you feel about male models?' as though 'models' and 'male models' are entirely different categories
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed misdirection. Hansel's ability to agree that models are vain and stupid (he is one) and then immediately ask about male models as a separate category is perfect absurdist logic and great character comedy. The structure — agree, pivot, implicitly exempt himself — is tight. High quotability; the rhythm of the exchange is very funny.

jokes.text: So I became... [extended pause while group waits] / What? / Bulimic. / You can read minds?
jokes.setup: Matilda is building to a painful confession about her eating disorder; there's a long, sincere pause as she struggles to say the word
jokes.punchline: Derek's 'You can read minds?' — he has apparently been thinking the word 'bulimic' and believes Matilda telepathically extracted it from his head
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel and arguably one of the great jokes in the film. The structure is impeccable: Matilda's sincere, emotionally loaded confession, the long dramatic pause, the word 'bulimic' — and Derek's response reveals he was ALSO thinking the word 'bulimic,' but for entirely different reasons, and interprets her saying it as mind-reading. The joke does everything: it characterizes Derek's terminal self-centeredness (he was thinking about bulimia as a weight-loss tool), it undercuts Matilda's sincere moment without being mean-spirited, and 'You can read minds?' is both absurd and completely in-character. Among the finest jokes in Ben Stiller's career. Comparable to anchor example quality.

jokes.text: It's when you throw up after every meal.
jokes.setup: Derek has just asked 'You can read minds?' in response to Matilda saying 'bulimic'
jokes.punchline: Matilda's patient, clinical definition of bulimia — delivered to an adult who apparently doesn't know what it is — highlights Derek's staggering ignorance of basic medical knowledge
jokes.explanation: The follow-up to joke #47 — Matilda's flat definition of bulimia to a grown man who doesn't know what it is extends the humiliation of Derek beautifully. The clinical tone in an emotionally raw moment is well-played.

jokes.text: See, you know what? This is exactly what you models do to people. You make them feel bad about themselves. / Matilda... / So what? I throw up after lots of meals. / So do I. It's a great way to lose pounds before a show.
jokes.setup: Matilda begins a righteous speech about how the fashion industry damages self-image
jokes.punchline: Derek and Hansel casually confirm they both vomit after meals for weight management — not as a disorder but as a standard professional practice, delivered with complete normalcy
jokes.explanation: A dark-comedy escalation that also works as sharp satire of fashion industry culture. Matilda's speech about the damage models do is immediately confirmed and negated by Derek and Hansel treating her eating disorder as a professional tip. 'It's a great way to lose pounds before a show' is delivered as helpfully as a fitness recommendation.

jokes.text: Wow. How did that affect you with guys? Did they not want to get busy with you? / Good point.
jokes.setup: Matilda has just shared her painful experience with bulimia in an emotionally vulnerable moment
jokes.punchline: Derek's response to a confession about an eating disorder is to immediately pivot to its effect on her sex life — and Hansel endorses the question as insightful
jokes.explanation: Derek's total inability to engage with emotional content — pivoting immediately from eating disorder to dating prospects — is a great character note. 'Good point' from Hansel is the kicker: Hansel's laid-back persona means he endorses everything uncritically, including this wildly inappropriate question.

jokes.text: Or lack thereof. / You mean, like, like you, like you... / Haven't really... / You haven't... / Done it... / Done it in a while, yeah.
jokes.setup: Matilda says she won't discuss her sex life 'or lack thereof' — accidentally revealing she hasn't had sex recently
jokes.punchline: Derek and Hansel tag-team finishing her sentence in a fumbling, excited relay that reveals they cannot believe a person could exist in a sexless state — and Matilda is forced to confirm it
jokes.explanation: The relay-confirmation of Matilda's celibacy is a good cringe-comedy bit. The broken, overlapping dialogue structure creates natural-feeling embarrassment, and the boys' inability to complete the sentence smoothly reflects their genuine discomfort with the concept of not having sex.

jokes.text: Okay, what's a while? Like, eight days? More? Try a couple years. / Oh, snap! / How do you live? How do you live? / Seriously. Do you service yourself ten times a day?
jokes.setup: Matilda has admitted it's been 'a while' since she's had sex; Derek guesses 'eight days'
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'eight days' to 'a couple years,' followed by Derek and Hansel's incredulous reactions ('Oh, snap!' / 'How do you live?') and Hansel's question about masturbation frequency — the revelation grows from mildly surprising to genuinely shocking to their worldview
jokes.explanation: Good escalation structure. 'Eight days' as Derek's guess is a perfect character note — that's his baseline for a 'long time.' 'Oh, snap!' from Hansel is funny in its unexpected currency. 'How do you live? How do you live?' — repeated for emphasis — captures their genuine bafflement.

jokes.text: I think we should get naked. / What? / Don't ask questions. Just give in to the power of the tea.
jokes.setup: The conversation has become increasingly uncomfortable; the tea has been subtly building as a plot device
jokes.punchline: Hansel's 'I think we should get naked' as a solution to interpersonal tension — delivered with total calm — and 'Give in to the power of the tea' confirming the tea is definitely drugged/hallucinogenic
jokes.explanation: A great button for the section. 'I think we should get naked' as Hansel's earnest solution to an awkward conversation is perfect character comedy — his go-to for any social problem is communal nudity. 'Don't ask questions. Just give in to the power of the tea' is highly quotable and delivers the payoff on the tea setup. Strong closer for this reel.

jokes.text: Hansel's peyote-fueled Mount Vesuvius story — he nearly 'dies' on the volcano, then remembers he's been smoking peyote for six straight days and realizes he was never there at all
jokes.setup: Hansel tells a harrowing, escalating story about rappelling down Mount Vesuvius and nearly dying from terror
jokes.punchline: He remembers he's been on peyote for six days and realizes he's never even been to Mount Vesuvius — the whole dramatic story was a hallucination
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully structured absurdist joke that works on multiple levels. The setup mimics the classic near-death epiphany story beat, then completely subverts it with the peyote reveal. The final line 'I've never even been to Mount Vesuvius' is perfect deadpan economy. It's deeply character-specific — only Hansel, the free-spirit surf-hippie archetype, would tell this story with zero irony. The escalation from terror to casual realization is excellently paced.

jokes.text: 'Cool story, Hansel.' / 'Thanks, Olaf.'
jokes.setup: Hansel finishes his absurd peyote hallucination story with zero self-awareness
jokes.punchline: Olaf's perfectly flat 'Cool story, Hansel' — and Hansel takes it as a sincere compliment, responding 'Thanks, Olaf'
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable exchanges in the film. 'Cool story, Hansel' became a cultural phrase because of its perfect sarcastic economy. Hansel's sincere 'Thanks, Olaf' adds another layer — he genuinely doesn't detect the deadpan dismissal. High quotability score because this phrase entered the vernacular.

jokes.text: Derek confessing he thinks he's falling for Matilda while casually embedded in a party involving Finnish dwarves and a Maori tribesman
jokes.setup: Derek wants to share a sincere romantic feeling about Matilda
jokes.punchline: The romantic moment he's describing occurred while Matilda was 'sandwiched between the two Finnish dwarves and the Maori tribesman' — delivered completely straight as a tender memory
jokes.explanation: Classic Zoolander absurdist escalation — the specificity of 'two Finnish dwarves and the Maori tribesman' is what makes this land. It's not vague weirdness; it's hyper-specific weirdness delivered with complete sincerity. The joke works because Derek frames it as a genuinely romantic moment, treating the insane context as utterly mundane.

jokes.text: 'What do you call that?' / 'I think you call that love, D-Bone.'
jokes.setup: Derek asks what you call the feeling of wanting to spend your life with someone you met while she was sandwiched between Finnish dwarves
jokes.punchline: Hansel solemnly declares 'I think you call that love, D-Bone' — genuine emotional wisdom delivered in the context of a bacchanalia, plus the nickname 'D-Bone'
jokes.explanation: The humor comes from treating genuinely absurd circumstances with sincere romantic gravity. 'D-Bone' as a nickname for Derek is a funny throw-in. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Derek complaining that Matilda didn't greet them properly: 'Easy. How about a Good afternoon, Derek and Hansel. Thanks for the freak fest last night?'
jokes.setup: Matilda bursts in urgently reminding them they have three hours to save Derek's life
jokes.punchline: Derek's priority is etiquette — she should have thanked them for the orgy before launching into the crisis briefing
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific to Derek's dim, socially oblivious self-importance. The word choice 'freak fest' is a funny understatement for whatever the previous night involved. His casual priority inversion — manners over assassination — is on-brand absurdist character comedy.

jokes.text: Derek's extended defense of the phrase 'Earth to': insisting it's not meant literally and they're not in a control tower trying to reach aliens
jokes.setup: Matilda says 'Earth to Matilda' sarcastically; Derek takes it literally and launches into an earnest clarification about figurative language
jokes.punchline: Derek explains, with great seriousness, that 'Earth to' doesn't mean they're literally in a control tower trying to reach outer-space aliens — a completely unnecessary and oblivious defense of a common idiom
jokes.explanation: A great Derek joke. His literal-minded explanation of a figurative phrase, delivered with absolute authority as if he's genuinely correcting a misunderstanding, is perfect character comedy. The specificity of 'control tower trying to reach outer space aliens' is funnier than a vague correction would be. This is Derek at his most earnestly idiotic.

jokes.text: 'Oh, snap! / A joke.' — the onlookers' reaction to Hansel's space-radio bit
jokes.setup: Hansel does the space-radio mime
jokes.punchline: Someone in the room reacts with 'Oh, snap! A joke.' — narrating the comedic beat as if it needed to be labeled, which is itself meta-funny
jokes.explanation: A secondary laugh that extends Hansel's space-radio bit. 'A joke.' as a flat announcement is mildly meta but works as a punctuation beat. Dependent on joke #8 — not strong on its own.

jokes.text: Derek's disguise plan — 'They won't be looking for... Not us' — presented as a stroke of genius
jokes.setup: Derek says he 'might just have an idea' and builds it up as brilliant strategic thinking about how they can sneak into Maury's
jokes.punchline: His plan is simply: wear a disguise. He presents this as an unprecedented masterstroke, complete with dramatic pauses.
jokes.explanation: Classic dim-protagonist joke — the elaborate build-up reveals a mundane solution. The dramatic pause before 'Not us' is funny because Derek is clearly proud of himself. Solid character comedy, nothing exceptional.

jokes.text: Hansel confirming he has a cosmetics case: 'Sure, I mean, just for touch-ups or whatever'
jokes.setup: Derek asks if Hansel has a cosmetics case as part of his disguise scheme
jokes.punchline: Hansel confirms he does, with casual sheepishness — 'just for touch-ups or whatever' — as if this is barely worth mentioning
jokes.explanation: Light character detail — Hansel carrying a cosmetics case while affecting a free-spirit persona is a nice touch. 'Just for touch-ups or whatever' is good deflection comedy. Supporting gag.

jokes.text: 'You is talkin' loco and I like it.'
jokes.setup: Derek reveals his plan to do his own makeup and tailoring disguise
jokes.punchline: Hansel endorses it with the grammatically broken 'You is talkin' loco and I like it' — delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: A highly quotable line. The grammatical incorrectness of 'You is talkin'' combined with the slang 'loco' captures Hansel's patois perfectly. Short, memorable, character-specific. Good economy.

jokes.text: The 'disguise' is revealed to be Derelicte — their cover is dressing as homeless people in the fashion show they're infiltrating
jokes.setup: Derek has been preparing elaborate disguises using his fashion expertise to infiltrate the Derelicte show
jokes.punchline: The 'disguise' is Derelicte fashion — they look like homeless people wearing garbage, which is also the fashion show's theme, meaning they fit in perfectly while also being ridiculous
jokes.explanation: Smart visual payoff to the disguise setup. The irony that the best disguise for infiltrating a homeless-chic fashion show is to dress like homeless people — using Derek's legitimate fashion skills — is a satisfying structural joke. The 'Welcome to Derelicte' announcement as the reveal is well-timed.

jokes.text: Hansel using spy radio protocol: 'Hansel calling Matil. Hansel calling Matil. We have entry. Repeat. We have entry.'
jokes.setup: Hansel is communicating with Matilda via earpiece while infiltrating the fashion show
jokes.punchline: He adopts full military radio protocol ('Hansel calling Matil,' 'We have entry. Repeat. We have entry.') with complete seriousness, as if this is a Special Forces operation
jokes.explanation: A reliable fish-out-of-water joke — the surf hippie going full military operator. Nicely played but not outstanding. The abbreviation 'Matil' instead of 'Matilda' is a small funny detail.

jokes.text: Derek apologizing over the spy radio for 'good-looking people like us' making Matilda throw up and feel bad about herself due to the bulimia
jokes.setup: Derek is on a covert mission communicating via spy earpiece; he has a sincere emotional message to deliver
jokes.punchline: His heartfelt apology for Matilda's bulimia centers on the idea that he and other attractive people caused it, and he 'feels really bad that good-looking people like us made you throw up' — a totally tone-deaf non-apology delivered with complete compassion
jokes.explanation: Derek's self-centered obliviousness reaches a perfect comedic peak — he's genuinely trying to empathize but can't help making it about how attractive he is. 'Good-looking people like us' is the key phrase: he's including himself as the problem while also complimenting himself. The timing during a covert infiltration operation makes it funnier. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Mugatu's backstory: kicked out of Frankie Goes to Hollywood for being the original guitar synth player, then invented the piano-key necktie in 1985
jokes.setup: An FBI contact delivers background intel on Mugatu to establish he's been in the fashion conspiracy for 30 years
jokes.punchline: Mugatu's humiliation origin story is that he was the founding guitar synth player of Frankie Goes to Hollywood — kicked out before they hit it big — and then invented the piano-key necktie in 1985 as his comeback
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully specific absurdist biography. The 'original guitar synth player for Frankie Goes to Hollywood' is a perfect detail — specific enough to feel real, ridiculous enough to be absurd. The piano-key necktie as his great invention (a real novelty item of the era) is an excellent callback to Mugatu's character. The choice of Frankie Goes to Hollywood is also a great joke given their most famous song becomes the trigger later. Rich with rewatch value.

jokes.text: Derek and Hansel struggling with the computer — 'Did you press that apple thing?'
jokes.setup: Derek and Hansel need to access files on a computer to find evidence
jokes.punchline: Their total technological incompetence — 'Did you press that apple thing?' referring to the Mac command key — is the ceiling of their computer knowledge
jokes.explanation: A reliable tech-incompetence gag. 'The apple thing' for the Mac Command key is a recognizable and character-appropriate joke. Functional comedy, not exceptional. Sets up the later 'it's in the computer' callback.

jokes.text: Derek's declaration after a beat of rage about the computer: 'Let's not lose our cool. Then we're no better than the machine.'
jokes.setup: Hansel and Derek have been struggling with the computer and presumably just had an outburst
jokes.punchline: Derek philosophically declares 'Let's not lose our cool. Then we're no better than the machine' — as if the computer is an adversary they must morally defeat
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent absurdist line. 'Then we're no better than the machine' is a phrase borrowed from anti-establishment philosophy, completely misapplied to a laptop computer. It's delivered with the earnestness of profound wisdom. High quotability — this is the kind of line people repeat. Economical and character-perfect.

jokes.text: Derek abandoning the mission because he's never been late for a show in his life and doesn't plan to start now
jokes.setup: Hansel urgently reminds Derek that if he goes to the show, he'll be brainwashed into assassinating the Malaysian prime minister
jokes.punchline: Derek's response: he's never been late for a show and doesn't plan to start now. Professional punctuality trumps potential murder.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Derek character moment. The model's professional code of conduct overriding self-preservation (or world peace) is exactly the right priority inversion for this character. 'Damn it, you're right' from Hansel is the perfect straight-man capitulation.

jokes.text: Hansel: 'Damn it, you're right.' — agreeing that Derek's punctuality ethics outweigh preventing an assassination
jokes.setup: Derek has just argued he can't miss the show because he's never been late
jokes.punchline: Hansel immediately concedes: 'Damn it, you're right' — treating professional punctuality as an airtight counter-argument to 'you'll commit murder'
jokes.explanation: The punchline to joke #19. Hansel's sincere capitulation makes the joke land harder — both men are equally oblivious. Economy is high: three words do the work.

jokes.text: Derek asking Hansel to deliver something to Matilda if anything happens to him — played as a dramatic farewell — then Hansel refuses to accept it as a death token
jokes.setup: Derek is about to walk into danger; he hands Hansel something meaningful and asks him to give it to Matilda if he doesn't make it — a classic action-movie farewell beat
jokes.punchline: Hansel refuses multiple times ('No. / Man.') and finally compromises: 'Let's just say I'll hold on to it till you get back' — subverting the dramatic death-flag moment with superstitious optimism
jokes.explanation: A smart parody of the action-movie farewell trope. Hansel's refusal to accept the 'death token' because doing so would seal Derek's fate is both superstitious and sweet. The compromise — 'I'll hold on to it till you get back' — is a good button on the bit.

jokes.text: News anchor announces 'veteran supermodel Derek Zootander' — mispronouncing his name
jokes.setup: A TV news anchor introduces Derek at the Derelicte show
jokes.punchline: 'Derek Zootander' — the film's running gag of people mispronouncing/misspelling Zoolander
jokes.explanation: A reliable running gag. 'Zootander' is a small but consistent joke. Works as a running gag payoff, not especially inventive on its own.

jokes.text: 'They're in the computer. It's so simple.' — Hansel's epiphany that the files are literally inside the physical computer
jokes.setup: Hansel needs to find secret files; Matilda told him they're in the computer
jokes.punchline: Hansel stares at the computer and has the revelation that the files are literally inside the physical machine — implying he may try to open it
jokes.explanation: One of the most beloved jokes in the film and a genuine comedic peak. 'They're in the computer — it's so simple' recontextualizes the obvious phrase 'in the computer' as a physical location. The delivery of profound breakthrough revelation when announcing the most basic fact in computing is perfectly absurdist. High quotability — this became iconic. The simplicity of the setup and the total commitment to the wrong interpretation make it exceptional. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: Hansel offers the distraught Matilda cantaloupe halves with cottage cheese because she 'seems a little tense'
jokes.setup: Matilda is in a full crisis — Derek is about to assassinate a world leader and they have minutes to stop it
jokes.punchline: Hansel interrupts to offer her a fruit and cottage cheese snack because she 'seems a little tense' — catastrophically misreading the room
jokes.explanation: Hansel's cosmic obliviousness in the face of crisis is perfectly in character. The specificity of 'cantaloupe halves with some cottage cheese' is funnier than a generic snack would be. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Matilda's trigger realization: 'Relax' — the Frankie Goes to Hollywood song is Derek's assassination trigger
jokes.setup: Hansel tells Matilda to 'relax' as she's stressed; she snaps back that the last thing she needs is to relax; then she freezes — 'That's it.'
jokes.punchline: The trigger is 'Relax' — the Frankie Goes to Hollywood song Mugatu came from. The word 'relax' just said in ordinary conversation unlocks the revelation. Pays off both the Mugatu backstory and Mugatu's 'just remember, relax' to Derek at the show.
jokes.explanation: A structurally outstanding comedic plot moment. The trigger being 'Relax' — the Frankie Goes to Hollywood song from Mugatu's humiliation — is a brilliantly earned reveal. It pays off multiple earlier jokes simultaneously (the Mugatu backstory, the casual use of the word by Hansel, Mugatu's loaded 'just remember, relax' to Derek). The fact that the discovery comes from Hansel casually saying it in conversation is perfect irony. High earned score because it rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Mugatu to Derek backstage: 'Just remember, relax.' — the trigger word delivered as innocent advice
jokes.setup: Mugatu appears to give Derek a friendly pep talk backstage before the show
jokes.punchline: 'Just remember, relax.' — the assassination trigger delivered with a warm smile as if it's coaching advice. Dramatic irony at its peak since we just learned this is the trigger.
jokes.explanation: Perfect dramatic irony. Coming immediately after Matilda's realization, Mugatu's 'just remember, relax' lands as a chilling punchline — we now know exactly what this means. The friendly-advice framing against the sinister subtext is excellent dark comedy structure. Very high rewatch value.

jokes.text: Derek to Maury: 'Don't you mean Good-bye?' — Derek reveals he knows Maury is behind the conspiracy
jokes.setup: Maury wishes Derek good luck before the show in what appears to be a standard farewell
jokes.punchline: Derek coolly responds 'Don't you mean Good-bye?' — revealing he knows Maury is in on the assassination plot. It's a movie-villain cool moment played with Derek's characteristic seriousness.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying dramatic beat that also works as comedy because of the absurdity of Derek pulling off a suave confrontation. The surprise of Derek being this perceptive undercuts his established dim persona in a funny way. 'I know it was you, Maury / it breaks my heart' is a parody of the crime-drama confession scene.

jokes.text: Mugatu greeting Matilda at the show: 'Glad you could join us, Kmart. Lucky for you, there is no dress code.'
jokes.setup: Matilda arrives at the fashion show dressed normally (not in couture)
jokes.punchline: Mugatu dismisses her as 'Kmart' — implying she's budget and unfashionable — then notes there's 'no dress code,' which is an insult masquerading as generosity
jokes.explanation: Classic Mugatu fashion-snob shade. 'Kmart' as a fashion insult is clean and punchy. 'Lucky for you, there is no dress code' as the gracious follow-through is a good structure. Character-specific to Mugatu's catty persona.

jokes.text: The Derelicte show opening with a model delivering the manifesto: 'I am vile spew of the wretched masses. I am really, really dirty. I am Derelicte!'
jokes.setup: The Derelicte fashion show begins — a high-fashion celebration of homelessness and poverty
jokes.punchline: The opening declaration treats garbage-aesthetic as profound art: 'I am vile spew of the wretched masses' delivered with fashion-show gravitas
jokes.explanation: The Derelicte show parody of pretentious fashion theatre is sharp satire. 'Vile spew of the wretched masses' as a fashion statement is excellent. The joke is on fashion's ability to aestheticize poverty with po-faced seriousness.

jokes.text: Derek on the runway, the trigger song plays — 'It's Relax!' — his face shifts to assassination mode
jokes.setup: Derek walks the Derelicte runway; Frankie Goes to Hollywood's 'Relax' begins playing; Matilda screams the revelation
jokes.punchline: The payoff of the entire brainwashing subplot — 'It's Relax!' — delivered as Derek's face goes blank and murderous. The absurdity of a pop song as an assassination trigger is the core joke.
jokes.explanation: The climactic payoff of a joke structure built across the entire film. 'Relax' as the trigger is funny because it's such an incongruous song for assassination programming — a disco-era pop song about sexual abandon as a murder command. The reveal is played with enough thriller energy to make the absurdity land harder. Excellent structural comedy.

jokes.text: Derek's internal brainwashing voice: 'Concentrate, Derelicte. Do not be distracted by the beautiful celebrities.'
jokes.setup: Derek is in assassination mode on the runway, trying to complete his programmed mission
jokes.punchline: His biggest obstacle to murdering the prime minister is being distracted by beautiful celebrities in the crowd — even as a killer, he's still fundamentally a model
jokes.explanation: Superb character integration. Derek's programming can override his mind but can't override his fundamental model instincts — even as a brainwashed assassin he's distracted by pretty celebrities. 'Do not be distracted by the beautiful celebrities' is a hysterically specific intrusion into a murder mission. This is exactly what Derek's character demands.

jokes.text: 'It's that damn Hansel! He's so hot right now! Popping and locking, fool!'
jokes.setup: Hansel breaks into the fashion show to interrupt Derek's assassination attempt by break-dance fighting
jokes.punchline: Mugatu's outraged reaction is 'It's that damn Hansel! He's so hot right now! Popping and locking, fool!' — equal parts villain fury and genuine fashion-world acknowledgment of Hansel's hotness, delivered in one breath
jokes.explanation: One of the most memorable lines in the film and a perfect comedic peak. Mugatu's villain fury is completely undermined by his inability to stop complimenting Hansel's hotness even in mid-crisis. 'Popping and locking, fool!' adds absurdist energy. The callback to 'he's so hot right now' in a moment of villain rage is structurally brilliant. Very high impact and quotability — this line became iconic.

jokes.text: Deadpan reporter covering the chaos: 'They're break-dance fighting.'
jokes.setup: Derek and Hansel are engaged in a chaotic physical confrontation on the runway to stop the assassination
jokes.punchline: A TV news reporter delivers the flat, clinical observation: 'They're break-dance fighting.' — the most understated possible description of the most absurd possible situation
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. The deadpan news-reporter framing applied to the most ridiculous situation imaginable is textbook perfect economy. 'They're break-dance fighting' became one of the most quoted lines from the film because it needs zero context — it's funny on its own. The clinical journalistic tone against chaotic absurdism is a brilliant contrast. Perfect economy score.

jokes.text: Hansel's public address to the crowd: 'Mugatu's a dick! He tried to brainwash Derek to kill the Claymation dude.'
jokes.setup: Hansel needs to publicly expose Mugatu's assassination conspiracy to a crowd of fashion elites
jokes.punchline: His expose begins with 'Mugatu's a dick!' and refers to the Malaysian prime minister as 'the Claymation dude' — an earnest and completely uninformed description
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character moment. Hansel's attempt at a principled public speech fails immediately with 'Mugatu's a dick!' then slides further with 'Claymation dude' for the Malaysian prime minister. The gap between the seriousness of the information and the crudeness of the delivery is the joke. 'Claymation dude' specifically is a great absurdist descriptor that reveals Hansel sees the prime minister as, essentially, an animated character.

jokes.text: Mugatu's rebuttal: 'Zoolander snapped because he's over the hill! He knew his career was over and he couldn't face it.'
jokes.setup: Mugatu is trying to spin the assassination attempt as a mental breakdown rather than a conspiracy
jokes.punchline: His cover story — that Derek snapped because his modeling career is over — lands as both a villain lie AND a credible fashion-industry shade
jokes.explanation: A functional plot beat with mild comedic value — Mugatu's spin is both sinister and funny because it's partially believable in context. Not a standout joke.

jokes.text: Hansel triumphantly holds up the laptop: 'We got 30 years of files right here in this computer! They're gonna bring you down!'
jokes.setup: Hansel is exposing Mugatu with computer evidence
jokes.punchline: He holds up the physical laptop computer — having apparently opened or extracted it — as the evidence. 'They're in the computer' pays off: he literally brought the computer as the evidence container.
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff to 'it's in the computer.' Hansel solved the problem by physically bringing the entire computer as the evidence, which is exactly what his literal interpretation of 'in the computer' would lead to. Structurally satisfying callback with strong earned score.

jokes.text: Mugatu somehow destroys the laptop computer files — 'Where did all the files go?' — Hansel is baffled
jokes.setup: Hansel presents the computer as evidence; Mugatu apparently destroys it
jokes.punchline: Hansel stares at the computer, baffled: 'Where did all the files go?' — he has no concept of data deletion or what just happened
jokes.explanation: A continuation of the computer-incompetence gag. Hansel's bewildered 'Where did all the files go?' treats data as a physical substance that has gone missing. Good running gag extension.

jokes.text: Matilda knocks out or defeats Mugatu and taunts him: 'You don't have the guts, Kmart!' / 'Wanna bet? And by the way, you were wrong about my outfit. It's the Cheryl Ladd Collection, and I got it at J.C. Penney. On sale.'
jokes.setup: Mugatu called Matilda 'Kmart' as a fashion insult when she arrived; now they're in physical confrontation
jokes.punchline: Matilda defeats Mugatu, then uses her victory speech to correct the fashion insult — it's not Kmart, it's the Cheryl Ladd Collection from J.C. Penney. On sale. This is her act of defiance.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff. Matilda's big triumphant moment is correcting which budget retailer her outfit came from — not Kmart, but J.C. Penney, and on sale — which deflates the heroic victory beat in the most fashion-conscious way possible. 'On sale' as the final button is perfect economy.

jokes.text: Maury's confession: 'I got a prostate the size of a honeydew, and a head full of bad memories. It's time to set things straight.'
jokes.setup: Maury confesses to being part of the fashion assassination conspiracy for 30 years
jokes.punchline: His reason for finally coming clean is not guilt or morality but a giant prostate and bad memories — the aging man's spiritual accounting
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Maury's 'prostate the size of a honeydew' as motivation for moral redemption is funny because it's both absurd and oddly human. The specific fruit — honeydew — is the right comedy word. Pairs health crisis with confession as moral equivalent. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Maury reveals: 'I got two words for you, sugar — Zip disc.' / 'The whole thing is in my den in Long Island.'
jokes.setup: Mugatu gloats that all the evidence was destroyed; Maury counters he has something
jokes.punchline: 'I got two words for you, sugar — Zip disc.' Then reveals a backup copy is in his den in Long Island — criminally incriminating evidence casually stored in a suburban den
jokes.explanation: 'I got two words for you, sugar' sets up 'Zip disc' as though it's something devastating — which a Zip disc is emphatically not by any dramatic standard. The bathos of a Zip disc as the great reveal is excellent. 'My den in Long Island' grounds a global conspiracy in the most mundane suburban space imaginable.

jokes.text: Maury calls his wife Sheila to bring the Zip disc — the call devolves into an argument about a casserole and traffic on the service road
jokes.setup: Maury dramatically calls his wife to retrieve crucial assassination-conspiracy evidence from their Long Island home
jokes.punchline: The call degenerates into directions about the service road, then into a fight about a casserole staying warm: 'For Christ's sake, it's a casserole, Sheila! It'll stay!'
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic moments in this reel. The collision of a world-historical conspiracy and a mundane married couple fight about a casserole is perfectly executed. The specificity of the service road directions, the Tupperware containers, and 'it's a casserole, Sheila! It'll stay!' hits exactly right. The escalation from global stakes to domestic argument is flawlessly structured. 'For Christ's sake, it's a casserole, Sheila!' is extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Mugatu's meltdown: 'Who cares about Derek Zoolander anyway? The man has only one look! Blue Steel, Ferrari, Le Tigre? They're the same face! Doesn't anyone notice this? I feel like I'm taking crazy pills!'
jokes.setup: Mugatu is unraveling as his conspiracy collapses; he pivots from assassination defense to genuine fashion criticism
jokes.punchline: His breakdown bypasses all the murder charges to focus on Derek's modeling inadequacy — one look, all the same face — culminating in 'I feel like I'm taking crazy pills!' as the cry of a man who has been professionally offended for years
jokes.explanation: The comedic peak of the entire reel and one of the great comedic meltdowns in film comedy. Mugatu's breakdown is perfect character comedy: he has genuine fashion grievances that have been subordinated to his assassination scheme, and in his moment of defeat they come pouring out. 'I feel like I'm taking crazy pills!' became one of the most quoted lines in modern comedy. The escalation — from 'who cares about Derek' to naming all three looks to demanding someone acknowledge the same-face problem — is masterfully structured. Character integration is nearly perfect: only Mugatu, the fashion-industry insider who orchestrated all this, would have this specific breakdown. Approaches the 9+ anchor calibration.

jokes.text: 'I invented the piano-key necktie! I invented it! What have you done, Derek? Nothing! You've done nothing! Nothing!'
jokes.setup: Mugatu's meltdown continues after his 'crazy pills' outburst; he now pivots to his own achievements
jokes.punchline: The piano-key necktie — the absurd invention from his humiliating backstory — is his proud legacy. 'I invented it!' against Derek's supposed nothingness is both pathetic and weirdly moving.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The piano-key necktie — established in Mugatu's ridiculous backstory as the consolation achievement of a failed musician — becomes his war cry in defeat. The patent absurdity of this being his proudest achievement against 'what have you done, Derek? Nothing!' is structurally brilliant. The escalating repetition of 'Nothing! You've done nothing! Nothing!' is funnier each time. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: Mugatu attempts to kill the prime minister himself with a poisoned hand dart, screaming 'Die, you wage-hiking scum!'
jokes.setup: Mugatu's plan has collapsed; in desperation he decides to do the assassination himself
jokes.punchline: 'Die, you wage-hiking scum!' — the assassination motivation is finally stated: economic policy. The prime minister was targeted for raising minimum wage. Mugatu has been orchestrating international murder over labor costs.
jokes.explanation: The conspiracy's motive reveal as a punchline — the whole assassination scheme was about cheap sweatshop labor costs. 'Wage-hiking scum' as a villain battle cry is excellent dark comedy. The reveal that this world-spanning conspiracy was motivated by minimum wage policy is both satirically sharp and absurdly petty.

jokes.text: Derek deflects the assassination dart with 'Magnum' — his ultimate look stops the dart mid-air
jokes.setup: Mugatu fires a poisoned dart at the prime minister; everyone expects Derek to react physically
jokes.punchline: Derek deploys 'Magnum' — his legendary, never-before-seen look — and it somehow physically deflects the dart. A male model's facial expression is used as a weapon.
jokes.explanation: The climactic payoff of the film's core joke. 'Magnum' — the legendary look — is so powerful it physically stops a dart. The idea that a facial expression is the ultimate weapon is a perfect absurdist comedic escalation that also resolves the plot. The crowd's reverent reaction ('Holy moly,' 'That's what I've been waiting for,' 'Dear God, it's beautiful') adds mock-epic weight. Excellent character integration: only Derek could save the world with a look.

jokes.text: Derek responds to Mugatu's 'one look' accusation by saying 'One look? One look? I don't think so!' — and then deploys Magnum, an entirely new look so powerful it blows everyone back.
jokes.setup: Mugatu has just argued that Derek only has one look, naming Blue Steel, Ferrari, and Le Tigre as all 'the same face.'
jokes.punchline: Derek defies this by deploying 'Magnum' — a new look so powerful it physically deflects a throwing star and causes awe from every witness. The response to the critique of one look is a mythic new look delivered with the gravity of a superhero move.
jokes.explanation: Structurally among the best jokes in the film. The payoff is built on multiple setups: (1) the film's running joke that Derek's looks are all the same, (2) Mugatu's specific 'one look' accusation, (3) Magnum teased earlier as a mythic unrealized look. The response — not an argument but a physical demonstration that is simultaneously absurdist (a facial expression that physically deflects weapons) and emotionally satisfying — is excellent comedy construction. 'There it is! Magnum!' from the crowd is a perfect button. The joke works because it takes Derek's vanity completely seriously while being completely insane.

jokes.text: Crowd reaction to Magnum: 'Holy moly.' 'Yeah, baby! That's what I've been waiting for!' 'Dear God. It's beautiful.' — multiple witnesses react to a facial expression with the awe of witnessing a miracle.
jokes.setup: Derek deploys Magnum — an extreme facial expression.
jokes.punchline: The crowd's reaction is that of people witnessing a religious event: 'Holy moly,' 'Dear God. It's beautiful.' The gap between stimulus (a facial expression) and response (spiritual awe) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The crowd's religious awe at a facial expression extends the Magnum joke well. 'Dear God. It's beautiful' is the standout reaction line. The escalation from 'Holy moly' to 'Dear God' mimics witnessing a genuine miracle, which is exactly the right tone for the parody.

jokes.text: Derek's father's reaction to seeing Magnum: 'That's my kid. That's my son. / Derek! I love that kid. Dumb as a stump, but I love him.'
jokes.setup: Derek's estranged coal-miner father watches his son heroically deploy Magnum to save the world
jokes.punchline: His proud parental declaration ends with 'Dumb as a stump, but I love him' — the warmest possible insult, and an accurate assessment
jokes.explanation: 'Dumb as a stump, but I love him' is excellent economy — it's simultaneously the most accurate and most affectionate description of Derek possible, delivered at his moment of triumph. The father's pride cutting immediately to the accurate assessment is good structure.

jokes.text: Derek's post-save priorities: Matilda congratulates him on saving the prime minister's life; Derek's response: 'I know. I turned left.'
jokes.setup: Matilda excitedly tells Derek he saved the prime minister of Malaysia; a heroic moment of acknowledgment
jokes.punchline: Derek's response prioritizes the personal breakthrough: 'I know. I turned left.' — the ability to turn left on the runway, his character flaw throughout the film, is what he's most proud of
jokes.explanation: A nearly perfect comedic beat. After saving a world leader's life, Derek's pride centers entirely on turning left — the film's central running gag about his modeling limitation. 'Right. Cool.' as his response to the assassination-prevention news, followed by 'I know. I turned left.' as the real victory, is flawless character comedy. Economy and character integration are both near-perfect. Among the best payoffs in the film.

jokes.text: The Derek Zoolander Centre for Kids Who Can't Read Good and Who Wanna Learn to Do Other Stuff Good, Too
jokes.setup: Derek introduces his new school in what appears to be a promotional PSA
jokes.punchline: The school's full name: 'The Derek Zoolander Centre for Kids Who Can't Read Good, and Who Wanna Learn to Do Other Stuff Good, Too' — grammatically wrong in multiple ways, with 'good' used where 'well' belongs, plus the vague aspirational 'Other Stuff Good, Too'
jokes.explanation: A beloved callback that also works as a standalone joke. The name is so perfect because it embeds the problem (kids who can't read good) in the solution (a school), commits the same grammatical error it promises to fix, and then trails off vaguely with 'and Other Stuff Good, Too.' The name being read twice with full gravity increases the effect. Very high quotability — the name became iconic.

jokes.text: Maury in the Derek Zoolander Centre promotional video — giving business advice about designer contracts
jokes.setup: The promotional video for the Centre shows reformed villain Maury now teaching business management
jokes.punchline: Maury's business lesson: 'The designer's got your nuts in a vice, offering you ten million plus three percent of every pair of underwear sold. What are you gonna do? Screw him! Hold out for more!' — a former criminal conspiracy architect now teaching models to negotiate ruthlessly
jokes.explanation: Maury's rehabilitation as a business ethics teacher is immediately undercut by his advice — 'screw him, hold out for more' is the same ruthless agent mentality, now applied positively. 'Your nuts in a vice' is vivid and characteristically blunt. Ironic that the man who orchestrated assassinations is now teaching models to negotiate underwear contracts.

jokes.text: Derek's Centre tagline: 'We teach you that there's more to life than just being really, really, really good-looking.'
jokes.setup: Derek delivers the Centre's inspirational mission statement to close the PSA
jokes.punchline: 'There's more to life than just being really, really, really good-looking.' — the number of 'really's betrays Derek's own uncertainty; the message is sincere but self-undermining
jokes.explanation: A satisfying thematic joke — Derek's inspirational message still centers on being good-looking. The triple 'really' is the character's vanity unconsciously leaking through. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Hansel announces he's taking the kids from the Derek Zoolander Centre to the George Washington Bridge for a lesson in base jumping
jokes.setup: The Centre is presented as an idyllic school; Hansel is now a faculty member
jokes.punchline: Hansel's lesson plan: take children to a bridge and teach them base jumping. 'Last one to the helicopter's a rotten egg!'
jokes.explanation: Perfect character button on Hansel — now a teacher, he's taking children on what is unambiguously a dangerous activity with cheerful irresponsibility. 'Last one to the helicopter's a rotten egg' implies they already have a helicopter standing by. Dark-funny and entirely Hansel.

jokes.text: Baby Derek Jr. makes 'his first look' — the infant does a Zoolander face, confirmed by proud parents
jokes.setup: Derek and Matilda have a baby; it's a happy family ending; the baby is shown
jokes.punchline: The baby's first developmental milestone is not walking or talking but performing a Blue Steel / Magnum look — the Zoolander legacy continues genetically
jokes.explanation: A wonderful closing visual gag. The film's central joke — Derek's signature looks — transferred to an infant as a hereditary trait is a perfect comedic button. 'He made his first look today' as the developmental milestone, delivered with parental pride, is exactly right. The audience seeing the baby do the face is the visual payoff.
